cards.title: Fix XSS with Context-Aware Output Encoding
cards.summary: Encode untrusted values separately for each output context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript string, URL) rather than escaping once at input.
cards.use_when: Reviewing or briefing developers on your storefront's product review fields, search results pages, or any template that echoes customer-supplied content.
steps: Identify every place customer-controlled data is echoed: product reviews, search query display, cart notes, custom engraving text, account names.

For each output location, apply the encoding matching that context: HTML-entity encoding in HTML body, attribute encoding inside attributes, JavaScript-string escaping inside script blocks, URL encoding inside hrefs.
Do not encode only at input or only once: a value written into a JavaScript string and then injected into HTML needs a second round of context-appropriate encoding.

Avoid deeply nested encoding chains where the same value passes through several languages or contexts; if a value must cross contexts, isolate it into a data attribute or JSON blob rather than embedding it inline.
Add a review step or linting rule so new template code that echoes user input gets a context check before release.
caveats: Encode at output, not just input; input filtering alone does not cover stored XSS in reviews or legacy data.
The source presenter calls deep nested encoding fragile and advises against it.

cards.title: Treat XSS Filtering Browser Features as Unreliable
cards.summary: Built-in reflected-XSS filters can be bypassed and even aid attackers, so do not count on them as your storefront's XSS defense.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether browser-level XSS filtering removes the need for server-side sanitization on your storefront's reflected input pages.
steps: Assume the browser's reflected-XSS filter may decide not to block an attack, or may be absent entirely, and that some bypasses can degrade into new attack classes.
Keep reflected XSS prevention on the server and in templates: encode output by context and validate input, rather than relying on the browser to strip script from URLs.
When testing your own storefront, use your own staging copy, not third-party sites.
Verify the current state of any named browser filter before relying on descriptions of it, since browser behavior and availability change.
caveats: The source describes this as a historical browser feature; verify its current status before citing it.
No filter, header, or browser feature alone guarantees XSS protection.

cards.title: Choose Between Content-Matched and Person-Targeted Ads
cards.summary: Content-based ad placement ties ad revenue to page quality; person-level tracking decouples ad value from content and shifts spend toward cheap, low-quality pages.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether your store should buy content-matched placements (relevant publishers, category pages) or behavioral audiences, and understanding why cheap inventory may outperform contextually relevant inventory on cost.
steps: For each campaign, state whether the targeting is against content (site, category, article context) or against the person (retargeting pools, lookalikes, cross-site profiles).
If using person-level targeting, compare effective cost per acquisition on premium publishers versus low-cost long-tail inventory, since the same user may be reachable much more cheaply elsewhere.

If you are the publisher or content site, recognize that person-level buying reduces the marginal value of quality content and pushes ad revenue toward cheap inventory; budget for this when forecasting content-driven revenue.

For sensitive product categories (e.g. health, fertility, baby, debt), suppress or exclude person-level audiences where downstream disclosure could harm the customer; the source cites a case where pregnancy-related targeting revealed a pregnancy to a family member.
caveats: The source's ad-economics discussion is the presenter's analysis, not a measured benchmark for your account.
Historical claims about which ad companies were profitable are dated; verify current figures.

cards.title: Plan for Third-Party Tags as Tracking Surfaces
cards.summary: A typical page loads around twenty third-party resources with tracking vantage, and roughly 70-80% of first-party URLs may be observable by one large analytics provider, per the cited census.
cards.use_when: Auditing your store's third-party script footprint or preparing a privacy review before adding another analytics, personalization or ad tag.
steps: Build an inventory of every third-party resource loaded on home, category, product, cart and checkout templates: analytics, pixels, chat, reviews, A/B tools, payment SDKs.
For each tag, record what data it can observe (URL, referrer, cookies, form contents) and whether it operates in the first-party context.
Prefer tags that make explicit contractual privacy commitments and avoid others; the source notes some CDNs publish such guarantees, though a published promise is not enforcement.
On checkout and account pages, minimize third-party scripts because those paths carry payment and identity data.
Re-audit after each new tool ships, since tags accumulate.
caveats: The census figures cited are several years old; treat the ~20 third parties and ~70-80% reach as directional, not current measurements.
A vendor privacy promise is a legal commitment, not a technical control.

cards.title: Understand Cookies and Third-Party Cookie Exposure
cards.summary: Cookies store a server-issued identifier returned on subsequent requests; the decision to send them on third-party image and iframe requests is what enabled cross-site tracking.
cards.use_when: Reviewing how your store's session, cart persistence and embedded third-party content handle cookies.
steps: Distinguish first-party cookies (set and read by your own domain) from third-party cookies (set by embedded resources); cart and login typically depend on first-party cookies.
Audit embedded third-party elements (images, iframes, widgets) and whether they receive cookies on your pages.
Set session cookies with HttpOnly and Secure attributes where applicable, and scope cookie domains narrowly, so attached third-party resources do not inherit your identifiers.

Recognize that third-party request cookie behavior has been restricted by several major browsers; verify current behavior in the specific browsers your customers use before assuming a cookie will or will not be sent.
caveats: Browser cookie policy changes frequently; treat any specific current restriction as subject to change.
Secure cookies prevent interception over plaintext, not tracking via other identifiers.

cards.title: Treat HSTS as a Security Feature That Can Be Repurposed
cards.summary: HSTS tells browsers to refuse plaintext requests to a domain, but subdomain-level rules can be abused to encode per-user bits.
cards.use_when: Reviewing domain and subdomain configuration for your store, especially if you control or delegate many subdomains.
steps: Deploy HSTS on your storefront domains deliberately, with care about preload and long max-age, since the setting is effectively sticky for returning visitors.
Inventory subdomains: because HSTS rules can be set per subdomain, a large delegated subdomain space becomes a tracking surface.
Restrict who can create subdomains and which parties can set headers on them, and retire unused subdomains.
Treat HSTS as transport protection only; it is not an anti-tracking or XSS control.
caveats: The subdomain encoding technique is discussed in the source as an observed abuse; do not rely on HSTS to prevent tracking.
HSTS configuration mistakes can lock users out of plaintext access; test before preloading.

cards.title: Assess Fingerprinting Risk on Your Storefront Analytics
cards.summary: Fingerprinting identifies a browser by combining many semi-unique attributes without storing anything, so it survives cookie clearing and third-party cookie blocking.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether removing third-party cookies actually reduces cross-site tracking of your store's visitors, or choosing an analytics approach for privacy-sensitive audiences.
steps: List the attributes your site or its tags can read: user-agent string, installed fonts, screen and window dimensions, canvas rendering output, audio rendering output, hardware concurrency, device memory, WebGL parameters, network type.
Treat any single attribute as non-identifying but the combination as highly identifying, and measure the combined entropy using a tool like the EFF's Panopticlick-style test against your own site.
If you are the publisher or merchant, note that fingerprinting continues working after cookies are cleared, so cookie-consent banners alone do not stop cross-site identification.
If you are evaluating privacy tooling, prefer approaches that address the combined fingerprint set rather than any single attribute.
caveats: Fingerprinting libraries and browser countermeasures change; check current implementations before acting.
The source discusses defensive countermeasures and open problems, not guaranteed solutions.

cards.title: Recognize Font Enumeration and Why It Is Hard to Fix
cards.summary: Pages infer installed local fonts by measuring whether applying a candidate font changes an element's size, giving one entropy bit per unusual font.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a privacy-preserving analytics or anti-tracking approach that claims to neutralize fingerprinting, to check whether font enumeration is addressed.
steps: Understand the mechanism: a page iterates a long list of font names, applies each to a test element, and checks if the rendered size changed; changed size implies the font is installed.
Accept that you cannot block reading element dimensions without breaking page layout, so a simple blocker is not the answer.

Consider the tradeoffs used in practice: treating local fonts as unavailable is acceptable for many Western sites but breaks some sites, especially in Asian-language contexts where local fonts are commonly required because system fonts are poor.
Alternative mitigations include mapping a language to a small permitted font set (trading privacy-set size for compatibility) and gating font access behind a permission prompt.
If you are auditing your own store, note that you almost certainly do not need local font enumeration for legitimate function.
caveats: The source notes defenses here are unsatisfying and standards work is contested.
Permission prompts help only when users decline; network traffic can still reveal font loading.

cards.title: Treat Canvas and Audio Fingerprinting as Unpredictable APIs
cards.summary: Canvas and audio rendering produce slightly different output across hardware and drivers, which can be hashed into an identifier the user never sees.
cards.use_when: Understanding what browser-based fingerprinting can extract from visitors to your store, or assessing what a privacy tool must suppress.
steps: Recognize that drawing operations rendered to a canvas can be read back as a blob or data URL and hashed; harmless uses exist (e.g. checking emoji support) but the same API serves fingerprinting.
Note that audio processing can be fingerprinted either by querying capability information or by generating a waveform and hashing subtle device-specific differences.
Treat these as hard-to-lie-about signals, since the rendering difference is inherent to the hardware and usually imperceptible to users.
When evaluating fingerprinting protections, check whether canvas and audio outputs are perturbed or blocked and whether that breaks legitimate functionality.
caveats: The source describes these techniques as observed in a widely used fingerprinting library; it does not claim they cover every device or browser.
Perturbing rendering can break legitimate canvas applications, so blanket blocking is a tradeoff.

cards.title: Audit Permissionless Hardware and Network APIs
cards.summary: Several APIs expose hardware and network characteristics without any permission prompt, giving every script on the page identifying data.
cards.use_when: Auditing third-party scripts on your store or judging how much identifying data your pages already leak by default.
steps: Enumerate what scripts on your pages can read without asking: hardware concurrency (CPU cores), Web Audio channel configuration, WebGL shader capabilities, an approximate device memory value, and network-touching APIs that reveal connection type and IP-adjacent details.
Treat these as available to every script on every page; there is no user-facing consent gate for them in the browsers described.
When adding a new script or SDK, include these APIs in the review of what that vendor can observe.
For privacy-sensitive storefronts, consider which scripts genuinely need hardware or network information and remove those that do not.
Verify the current standardization and browser support for each API before relying on any specific one.
caveats: Standardization status varies; some APIs are non-standard or Chromium-only per the source.
These APIs are not the only identifying sources; they are a subset.

cards.title: Treat Viewport Size as the Hardest Fingerprint to Fake
cards.summary: True visible window dimensions are difficult to spoof without breaking layout, making them among the most identifying browser attributes.
cards.use_when: Assessing how much identifying information your responsive storefront design indirectly exposes, or evaluating anti-fingerprinting tooling.
steps: Distinguish between querying window dimensions via JavaScript (easy to override) and inferring them by measuring whether an image displays or how text flows (hard to override without breaking rendering).
Recognize that because the hard method cannot be faked without breaking pages, viewport size tends to be a strong identifying signal.
When designing responsive storefront layouts, be aware that layout APIs used to measure rendering can serve as fingerprinting side channels.
If evaluating privacy tooling, check whether it addresses dimension-based identification, not only JavaScript-visible values.
caveats: Countermeasures here are limited; the source calls it the hardest case.
Any specific tool's handling of viewport fingerprinting should be verified for the current version.

cards.title: Use Hashing Aggregation to Reason About Poisoning Fingerprints
cards.summary: Fingerprinting implementations typically hash many inputs into one combined value; corrupting one input can invalidate the whole fingerprint.
cards.use_when: Evaluating anti-fingerprinting approaches or deciding which single signal a protection should target when full masking is impractical.
steps: Understand the implementation pattern: each input (font set, viewport, canvas output) is separately hashed, then all hashes are combined into one stored value.
Recognize the implication: altering any one contributing input changes the combined output, so you do not necessarily need to neutralize every signal.
Treat this as a reason to prioritize which signal is cheapest to randomize reliably without breaking functionality, rather than trying to mask all signals.
Do not assume this always works: the source notes it is often, not universally, true, and sophisticated implementations may be resilient.
caveats: The source explicitly qualifies this as 'not always true', so treat it as a heuristic.
Randomizing an input may degrade legitimate functionality such as localization or rendering.

cards.title: Account for Cookie Syncing Across Identifiers
cards.summary: Tracking consolidates multiple cookie identifiers into one person by matching them with fingerprint data when a cookie is new or unrecognized.
cards.use_when: Understanding why clearing cookies or blocking third-party cookies alone does not sever an existing cross-site profile of your store's visitors.
steps: Understand the pattern: when a tracker sees a recognized cookie, it stops; when it sees an unrecognized cookie, it fingerprints the browser and links the new cookie to the existing profile.
Recognize that this makes cookie clearing insufficient on its own to prevent identity linking across sites.
For analytics and personalization on your store, avoid embedding tracking vendors whose linking behavior you cannot inspect, since identifiers you set may be joined to external profiles.
Prefer first-party measurement where practical, and document which identifiers (cookies, local storage) your own stack writes so you can reason about linkage risk.
caveats: The source describes this as an extremely difficult problem to work around; do not present a simple fix as guaranteed.
Specific tracker behavior changes; verify current practices of any vendor you use.

cards.title: Check New Tags for Identity-Linking Risk Before Adding
cards.summary: Any script with broad page access may join your visitors' identifiers to external profiles; review new store tools for this before shipping.
cards.use_when: Before adding a personalization, reviews, chat, A/B testing, or attribution vendor to your storefront.
steps: Ask what identifiers the tool reads and writes, and whether it operates across other sites where it already has a foothold.
Check whether the vendor claims to fingerprint or sync cookies with other data; independent value does not require cross-site identity linkage.
Prefer tools that operate with limited page access and explicit privacy commitments, and confirm whether those commitments are contractual.
For account and checkout pages, restrict script access to data beyond what the tool needs to function.
Re-check after vendor updates, since a tool's data collection can change post-integration.
caveats: Vendor claims and practices change; verify rather than assuming.
Independent functionality does not guarantee no cross-site linkage.

cards.title: Set Up a Repeatable External Script Review
cards.summary: Consistent periodic review of embedded scripts, APIs used, and identifiers collected keeps tracking exposure from quietly expanding as the store changes.
cards.use_when: Scheduling a recurring privacy and security review of your ecommerce site, or onboarding a new developer to review standards.
steps: Establish a checklist that covers every template: home, category, product, search results, cart, checkout, account, order confirmation.
For each template, record the third-party resources loaded, what data they can read (URL, cookies, form fields, hardware signals), and whether they require permission.
Note which screens reveal sensitive product interest (health, fertility, baby, financial) where person-level targeting could create downstream disclosure harms.
Review on a recurring cadence and after each release that adds a tag, script, or integration.
Spot-check against an available fingerprint-testing tool to see how identifying your own site's configuration makes an average visitor, without assuming any single tool covers all signals.
caveats: Specific testing tools and their signal coverage change; verify current versions.
Automated tests reveal what your own rendering exposes, not what external trackers can infer from elsewhere.
